title: US payment speed changes transfer behavior and deposit demand
source_unit: US depositor transaction, bank-transfer, county rollout, and deposit-demand measures

observations.period: Transaction-level data from millions of depositors; transfer-speed variation and Zelle staggered rollout

denominator.unit: millions of US depositors; exact study count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

transfer_delay_exposure.unit: matched debit-to-credit transfer delay; directionally measured, exact estimate not disclosed in the abstract

payment_speed_and_transfer_frequency.unit: faster transfers are associated with more transfers

payment_speed_and_deposit_growth.unit: faster payments reduce deposit growth in the study's estimates

observations.method: Transaction-level matching of debits and credits across accounts held by the same depositor, combined with county-level exposure to Zelle's staggered rollout and a calibrated deposit-management model.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not report effect sizes, sample dates, or the full identifying assumptions. The rollout design supports a causal research strategy, but the abstract alone cannot establish magnitude, household welfare, bank competition, or universal effects across payment methods.
observations.subgroup: US depositors and counties exposed at different times to Zelle; transaction and county units are not interchangeable with all households or all banks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Faster payments may change deposits through liquidity management, account substitution, interest rates, consumption volatility, or bank product selection; lower deposit growth is not automatically lower household security.

related_sources.claim: US credit-card lending economics and market-power comparator.
US household liquidity, payment, and financial-adaptation context.

boundary: This record identifies a US payment-infrastructure mechanism linking transfer delay, depositor activity, deposit growth, and monetary transmission. It does not report the abstract's omitted effect sizes, establish a same-household welfare change, measure fraud or remedy, or show that faster payments improve resilience, trust, or consumer power.
